rationale: A wins because it keeps the story on the evidence and makes proof gates do real work. Its best line, "Toast wants to be its restaurants' bank. It won't say how many of them default," turns the undisclosed default-rate fact into a reporter-shaped accountability angle without inventing a scandal. B has useful bones, but "Toast's profits are coming from lending and payroll" sells a payroll-profit claim the update does not give it, and that is how a pitch gets killed in edit.
gaps_in_A: "turning point-of-sale into the operating account" overreaches. The update supports lending and payroll bundling, not an operating-account thesis.
"This story will likely get written whether or not Toast pitches it" is editorial chest-thumping without evidence. Keep the risk, lose the fortune-telling.

"How one restaurant repaid its POS provider a slice of every day's sales" is a strong shape, but no named operator or repayment experience is in the update. A labels the proof gap, but this is still a sourcing assignment, not a ready pitch.
"sending any of them without a position on defaults" over-applies the default-rate gate. Payroll needs product proof and a customer first; defaults matter mainly to the lending angles.
gaps_in_B: "Toast's profits are coming from lending and payroll" is not grounded. The update says lending and fintech are higher-margin than hardware; it does not say payroll is driving profit.
"Toast just disclosed" invents source texture. The prompt gives facts; it does not say this was a disclosure, earnings release, or investor-day statement.
"a lender wearing a software company's branding" is a cute line with too much caffeine. Toast offers cash advances, but the update does not justify reducing the company to a lender.
"fees keep piling up" implies the new lending/payroll bundle adds fee burden. The update only says some owners have complained about Toast's fees, not that these products caused pile-on costs.
